blue-palo-verde.name: Blue Palo Verde
blue-palo-verde.origin: Sonoran Desert — Arizona, southeastern California, Baja and Sonora
blue-palo-verde.description: Arizona's state tree, and the one that makes a desert yard read as desert. The whole trunk and every branch are smooth blue-green and photosynthesize on their own, so the tree stays alive-looking even after it drops its tiny leaves in drought or cold. For a few weeks each spring it disappears under a solid mass of yellow flowers heavy enough to carpet the ground beneath it. Fast growing, deeply drought tolerant, and multi-trunked by nature — it casts a light, moving shade that other plants can actually grow in, which is why saguaros so often start life under one. Give it real room: mature spread matches or exceeds its height, and the wood is brittle enough that it wants clearance from roofs and drives.

desert-ironwood.name: Desert Ironwood
desert-ironwood.description: One of the Sonoran Desert's great nurse trees and among the longest-lived — individuals can persist well over a century. Ironwood carries a dense canopy of small blue-grey leaflets on gnarled grey bark, and flushes lavender-pink pea flowers in late spring. Its wood is famously heavy and hard, sinking in water. Slow but tough as nails, it casts genuinely useful filtered shade, shelters understory plantings, and anchors a native design as a long-term signature tree. Give it room and almost no supplemental water once established.

honey-mesquite.name: Honey Mesquite
honey-mesquite.description: A native desert tree prized for its feathery, fine-textured canopy that casts dappled shade without completely blocking sunlight. Its deep taproot makes it exceptionally drought tolerant once established — one of the most water-wise shade trees available for arid climates. Produces fragrant yellow flower spikes in spring followed by long seed pods enjoyed by wildlife. The gnarled trunk and graceful canopy give landscapes a natural, rugged character.

path-light.name: Path Light
path-light.description: A classic hat-style path light on a slim stake, throwing a soft warm pool about 5 ft across onto the walkway below — the lamp sits up inside the shade, so you see the light and not the bulb. Space them 5 to 7 ft apart so the pools just touch, and stagger sides for rhythm rather than a runway. Switch to Night Mode to see the glow; in daylight it reads as a slim dark fixture.

desert-willow.name: Desert Willow
desert-willow.description: Not a true willow but a member of the trumpet-creeper family, prized across the Southwest for its long, willowy leaves and orchid-like trumpet flowers in pink, burgundy, and white. It blooms heavily from late spring through fall, drawing hummingbirds all season, then drops its leaves for a sculptural winter silhouette of twisting trunks. Fast-growing, deeply drought tolerant, and happy in reflected heat, it works as a patio shade tree, a screening multi-trunk, or a flowering accent near seating. Prune to shape while young to build good structure.

texas-ebony.name: Texas Ebony
texas-ebony.description: A dense, dark evergreen with zigzagging thorny branches and small glossy compound leaflets that hold their deep green through the worst of summer. Texas Ebony grows slowly into a heavy, rounded canopy that casts genuinely deep shade — one of the few desert-adapted trees that reads lush rather than airy. Creamy, fragrant puffball flowers appear through summer, followed by thick woody seed pods. Its density and thorns make it an excellent privacy or barrier tree; give it clearance from walkways and expect to limb it up over a patio. Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established.

mulga.name: Mulga
mulga.description: The most useful evergreen in the low-water palette: a neat, upright tree of silver-gray foliage that holds its colour and its shape through the worst of summer on almost no irrigation. The "leaves" are phyllodes — narrow, leathery blades that give the canopy a fine, misty texture and read blue-silver against a wall or a dark backdrop. Slow-growing to 15–20 ft with a rounded crown, it stays in scale beside a single-storey house, drops very little, has no thorns, and throws short yellow rod flowers in spring and after summer rains. Use it singly as a small shade or accent tree, in a row as a screen, or anywhere a designer wants year-round silver without the litter or the water bill of an olive. Full sun, sharp drainage, hardy to the mid-teens.
mulga.bloom: Spring, and after summer rains — short yellow rods

chaste-tree.name: Chaste Tree
chaste-tree.origin: Mediterranean and western Asia — long naturalized across the Southwest
chaste-tree.description: The desert's answer to a lilac, and one of the few low-water trees that flowers all summer instead of for two weeks in spring. 'Shoal Creek' is the cultivar worth specifying: longer, deeper blue-purple spikes than the seedling form, and nearly sterile, so it drops far less litter and doesn't seed itself around. The leaves are grey-green and palmate — five to seven narrow fingers that read soft and tropical from a distance while asking for desert water. Naturally multi-trunked and vase-shaped, which makes it a natural patio or courtyard tree; it can be trained to a single trunk if a cleaner line is wanted. Deciduous and late to leaf out, so plan for a bare structural silhouette from December through March. Hardy well below anything Arizona sees, fast to fill in, and it will bloom repeatedly if the spent spikes are cut back after each flush.

orange-tree.name: Orange Tree
orange-tree.description: A classic citrus tree that brings fragrance, color, and edible fruit to residential landscapes. Its glossy dark green foliage, fragrant white blossoms, and bright orange fruit make it one of the most ornamentally versatile trees available. Thrives in full sun with regular watering and well-drained soil. Ideal for warm, frost-light climates. Often used as a specimen tree, espalier, or productive element in a kitchen garden design.

leatherleaf-acacia.name: Leatherleaf Acacia
leatherleaf-acacia.description: A tough, upright evergreen with thick, round grey-green phyllodes that feel genuinely leathery — an unusual, coin-like texture among desert plants. It carries small yellow puffball flowers after rain and forms a dense screen with almost no care, tolerating heat, reflected sun, alkaline soil, and long dry spells. Trained up it becomes a handsome small patio tree; left alone it makes one of the most reliable privacy hedges available for low-water designs. Very low litter and no thorns.

arizona-boulder.name: Arizona Boulder
arizona-boulder.description: A natural Arizona desert boulder scanned on-site, with weathered surfaces and authentic Sonoran character. Use it as a focal anchor, border accent, or dry riverbed element. Its rugged form pairs beautifully with cacti, agave, and low-water perennials. Zero maintenance and effectively permanent once placed.

mexican-fan-palm.name: Mexican Fan Palm
mexican-fan-palm.description: The most widely planted palm in the American Southwest, the Mexican Fan Palm is prized for its dramatic height and slender silhouette. Its long fronds fan out at the crown, creating an unmistakably tropical skyline presence. Fast growing and extremely drought tolerant once established, it thrives in full sun and poor soils. Commonly used in rows along driveways, property borders, and commercial streetscapes for bold vertical impact.

madagascar-palm.name: Madagascar Palm
madagascar-palm.description: Not a true palm at all but a succulent, the Madagascar Palm carries a thick silver-gray trunk armored in spines, topped by a rosette of long strap-shaped leaves that gives it an unmistakable palm-like silhouette. It reads as a living sculpture — a strong vertical accent beside entries, courtyards, and pool decks, or in a container where its form can be seen in the round. Extremely drought tolerant and slow growing, it wants full sun and sharp drainage. Fragrant white flowers appear at the crown on older plants. Frost sensitive below about 30°F and heavily spined — site it out of walkways.

texas-sage.name: Texas Sage
texas-sage.origin: Chihuahuan Desert — West Texas and northern Mexico
texas-sage.description: Also sold as Texas Ranger or barometer bush, and the second name is the honest one: it reads humidity and erupts into bloom a day or two after a monsoon rain, covering itself so completely in purple that the silver foliage disappears. Between flushes it is still doing work — soft woolly grey-white leaves that hold colour year-round and contrast with everything green around them. It is one of the toughest shrubs in the Southwest palette: full sun, reflected heat, alkaline soil, and essentially no supplemental water once established. Left alone it builds a loose, naturally rounded form and blooms hardest; shear it into a formal ball and you trade most of the flowers for the shape, so give it the room to be itself.

green-hopseed.name: Green Hopseed
green-hopseed.origin: Arizona native — Sonoran Desert foothills and chaparral, pantropical
green-hopseed.description: The workhorse screen of the desert palette: a fast, upright evergreen that goes from a 5-gallon whip to a 10 ft privacy hedge in three or four seasons on almost no water. Narrow, glossy, willow-like leaves give it a fine texture that takes shearing into a formal wall or, left alone, builds a loose vase of arching stems. Inconspicuous spring flowers are followed by papery, winged seed capsules that flush pink-tan and rattle in the wind through summer. Plant it on 4–5 ft centres along a fence or property line, use a single specimen as a soft backdrop for cactus and agave, or limb it up into a small multi-trunk tree. Full sun, sharp drainage, hardy to the mid-teens — one of the few native hedges that looks good in August.
green-hopseed.bloom: Spring (inconspicuous) — pink-tan winged seed capsules through summer

jojoba.name: Jojoba
jojoba.description: A dense, leathery evergreen shrub with thick blue-green leaves held upright, edge-on to the sun — a natural adaptation that keeps it looking fresh through brutal summers. Jojoba is the source of the liquid wax pressed from its seeds, and its tidy, naturally rounded habit makes it one of the best low-water screening and hedging shrubs for the desert. It takes shearing well, needs essentially no supplemental water once established, and stays evergreen year-round. Plants are male or female; only females set the seed capsules.

little-john-bottlebrush.name: Little John Bottlebrush
little-john-bottlebrush.description: A compact, dwarf evergreen shrub prized for its dense, mounding habit and fine blue-green foliage. New growth emerges with a bronze-purple tint, and in spring and summer it produces the classic crimson bottlebrush flowers that draw hummingbirds and bees. Little John stays naturally small and tidy without much pruning, making it a favorite for low hedges, borders, foundation plantings, and containers. Exceptionally heat and drought tolerant once established, it thrives in full sun and well-drained soil.

yellow-bells.name: Yellow Bells
yellow-bells.origin: Southern United States to South America
yellow-bells.description: A fast-growing, sun-loving shrub prized for its profuse clusters of bright golden, trumpet-shaped flowers that bloom from spring through fall. Its lush green serrated foliage and continuous color make it a favorite for desert and Mediterranean landscapes, where it attracts hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, Yellow Bells works beautifully as an informal hedge, screen, or colorful focal point. Can be kept shrubby with pruning or trained into a small multi-trunk tree.

yellow-lantana.name: Yellow Lantana
yellow-lantana.description: The gold standard for Arizona colour, and the lantana most likely to still be blooming in August. 'New Gold' mounds rather than trails, building a dense rounded cushion smothered in clear golden-yellow clusters from spring until frost — no deadheading, no fading to orange, no seed set to slow it down. It takes full reflected heat off pavement and block walls, wants poor soil and little water, and holds its shape better than the trailing types, which makes it the safer choice along walks and driveway edges. Butterflies work it constantly. Shear it hard in late winter to clear frost damage and keep the centre from going woody; it rebounds fast. Evergreen in mild winters and root-hardy well below that.

saguaro.name: Saguaro
saguaro.description: The undisputed icon of the Sonoran Desert, the Saguaro is the largest cactus in the United States and one of the most recognizable plants on earth. Its tall columnar trunk and upward-reaching arms define the Arizona landscape. Incredibly slow growing — a 6-foot specimen may be 50–75 years old — and federally protected in Arizona. Adding a mature Saguaro to a landscape is a rare and premium statement piece. White flowers bloom at the crown in late spring, followed by edible red fruit prized by wildlife and indigenous peoples for centuries.

organ-pipe.name: Organ Pipe
organ-pipe.description: A many-armed columnar cactus that branches from the base rather than the trunk, sending up a candelabra of ribbed green columns that reads as pure Sonoran Desert. Slower and more sculptural than a saguaro and legal to plant without a permit, it makes a superb evening focal point — the large white flowers open only at night and close by mid-morning, followed by sweet red fruit. Frost is its one limit: it wants a warm microclimate and a south or west exposure in the low desert. Give it room to widen, and light it from below to throw the rib shadows.

totem-pole.name: Totem Pole
totem-pole.description: A spineless, sculptural columnar cactus prized for its smooth, hand-carved look. Unlike most cacti, the Totem Pole bears no spines or sharp ribs — its blue-green columns are instead covered in irregular, rounded knobs that give it a totem-like silhouette. A slow-growing monstrose form of the Senita cactus, it makes a striking architectural focal point in desert and modern landscapes. Extremely drought tolerant and low maintenance, though slightly frost-sensitive. Pairs beautifully with boulders, agave, and fine gravel.

mexican-fence-post.name: Mexican Fence Post
mexican-fence-post.description: A tall, columnar cactus with distinctive white-ribbed margins that give it a striking striped appearance. Grows in tight, upright columns and is commonly used as a living fence or privacy screen in desert landscapes — hence the name. Produces small pink flowers along the ribs, followed by edible red fruit. Extremely low maintenance and one of the most architectural cacti available for residential design.

uplight.name: Uplight
uplight.description: A stake-mounted LED uplight for accenting trees, cacti, and walls after dark. Place it at the base of a plant and use the rotation gesture to aim the tilted head. Switch to Night Mode to see the warm 2700K beam light the foliage — in daylight the fixture shows as a small dark stake with an amber lens.

argentine-toothpick.name: Argentine Toothpick
argentine-toothpick.description: A striking tree-like cactus that forms a thick central trunk topped with a dramatic crown of upward-reaching blue-green columns. Its long white spines catch light beautifully, giving it an almost luminous quality in the landscape. The Argentine Toothpick makes a bold architectural statement as a specimen plant or grouped in a desert composition. Extremely drought and heat tolerant, it thrives in the low desert with virtually zero maintenance once established.

golden-barrel.name: Golden Barrel
golden-barrel.description: One of the most iconic desert cacti, the Golden Barrel forms a perfect globe of bright golden spines that catch sunlight beautifully. A classic focal point in Sonoran and Mediterranean-style landscapes, it is commonly grouped in odd numbers for dramatic effect. Slow growing and extremely long lived, it requires virtually no maintenance once established. Toxic to pets and has sharp spines — place away from high-traffic areas.

fire-barrel.name: Fire Barrel
fire-barrel.description: A bold, globe-shaped barrel cactus prized for its deep vertical ribs and dramatic reddish spines that glow when backlit by the sun. A classic focal point in Sonoran and Mediterranean-style landscapes, it pairs beautifully with fine gravel, boulders, and golden barrels in odd-numbered groupings. Slow growing and extremely long lived, it requires virtually no maintenance once established. Sharp spines — place away from high-traffic areas.

santa-rita-prickly-pear.name: Santa Rita Prickly Pear
santa-rita-prickly-pear.origin: Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts, Arizona and Mexico
santa-rita-prickly-pear.description: The most colorful of the desert prickly pears, Santa Rita produces broad, spineless-looking blue-green pads that flush deep purple-lavender in cold weather and drought — the stress response that gives it its signature color. Bright yellow blooms open along the pad edges in spring, followed by red-purple fruit. It forms a wide, upright clump over time and reads as a bold sculptural mass against gravel, boulders, and low-water perennials. Extremely heat and drought tolerant with essentially no maintenance once established. The pads carry fine glochids (hair-like barbed spines) — site it away from walkways, pool decks, and play areas.

agave-americana.name: Agave Americana
agave-americana.description: A dramatic architectural succulent that anchors any landscape with bold, symmetrical form. Its blue-gray leaves are broad and rigid with sharp terminal spines, making it a striking focal point. Agave Americana is monocarpic — it blooms once after 10–30 years, sending up a towering flower stalk up to 25 feet tall, then dies. Offsets (pups) ensure the colony lives on. Extremely drought and heat tolerant.

artichoke-agave.name: Artichoke Agave
artichoke-agave.description: The Artichoke Agave forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of broad, blue-gray leaves that overlap like the bracts of an artichoke. Compact and slow growing, it stays smaller and more refined than most agaves, making it an ideal focal point for tighter spaces, containers, and modern desert designs. Each leaf is tipped with a dark terminal spine and edged with fine teeth. Exceptionally drought tolerant and notably cold hardy, it thrives in full sun and well-drained soil with virtually no maintenance.

flat-boulder.name: Flat Boulder
flat-boulder.description: A low-profile desert boulder with a broad, flat surface that blends naturally into the landscape. Ideal for stepping stone paths, dry riverbed accents, or anchoring plant groupings at ground level. Its horizontal form contrasts beautifully with the vertical lines of cacti and agave. Zero maintenance and extremely long lasting — a timeless hardscape element in any Southwest design.

blue-glow-agave.name: Blue Glow Agave
blue-glow-agave.description: One of the most refined agaves available, and the reason it shows up in so many contemporary desert designs: a tight, symmetrical rosette of smooth blue-green leaves, each edged in a thin translucent red-and-gold margin that lights up when the sun sits behind it. It stays small and solitary — no pups crowding the base — which makes it reliable in a row, in a pot, or as a single accent beside a walk. The terminal spine is short and the leaf edges are smooth, so it is safer than most agaves near seating and paths. Full sun to light afternoon shade, sharp drainage, and very little water. Like all agaves it flowers once and then dies, but that is typically a decade or more out.
blue-glow-agave.bloom: Rarely — monocarpic, flowers once at the end of its life

black-tip-agave.name: Black Tip Agave
black-tip-agave.description: A dramatic, symmetrical rosette of hundreds of narrow, arching deep-green leaves, each tipped in a fine dark spine and edged with curling white filaments. Unlike the heavy blue agaves, this one reads soft and fountain-like, holding a nearly perfect sphere of foliage without offsetting. It makes an exceptional container specimen or a focal accent in gravel and boulder plantings, and its spineless margins make it safe alongside walkways. Extremely drought tolerant once established; appreciates a little afternoon shade in the hottest low-desert exposures.

twin-flowered-agave.name: Twin-flowered Agave
twin-flowered-agave.description: The Twin-Flowered Agave forms a strikingly dense, symmetrical fountain of hundreds of slender, deep green leaves, each edged with fine curling white filaments that catch the light. Unlike most agaves, its narrow, flexible leaves carry no harsh terminal spine, giving it a soft, almost grass-like texture that reads beautifully in modern and naturalistic desert designs. Compact and slow growing, it makes an elegant container or focal specimen. Exceptionally drought and heat tolerant, it thrives in full sun and well-drained soil with virtually no maintenance.

desert-spoon.name: Desert Spoon
desert-spoon.origin: Chihuahuan Desert — southeastern Arizona, New Mexico, West Texas and northern Mexico
desert-spoon.description: A perfect sphere of narrow blue-gray blades, each edged in fine golden teeth, that reads as a single sculptural object from any angle — the desert's answer to a boxwood ball, without the water or the shearing. Desert Spoon grows slowly to a 4–5 ft rosette and in age lifts itself on a short trunk skirted in dry leaves; in early summer a mature plant sends up a single 10–15 ft flower pole that stands for months. Use it in threes and fives to stitch a planting together, singly as a focal point against gravel or a wall, or in a row where it makes a formal rhythm with no maintenance. The teeth are sharp enough to keep it a step back from paths. Full sun, hard drainage, drought-proof once established, and hardy well below anything Arizona sees.
desert-spoon.bloom: Late spring – summer, a single tall flower pole (not modelled)

red-yucca.name: Red Yucca
red-yucca.origin: Chihuahuan Desert — central and west Texas into northern Mexico
red-yucca.description: Not a yucca at all, and the most forgiving plant in the desert palette. A tight fountain of narrow blue-green blades throws coral-red tubular flowers on slender arching spikes for months on end, starting in spring and often repeating until frost — hummingbirds work it all summer. The blades are soft-tipped and completely harmless, which is the reason it goes where an agave or a true yucca cannot: along walks, beside pool decks, under windows, in parking islands and median strips. It takes reflected heat off paving, full sun, hard drought and cold well below anything Arizona sees, and it stays the same size for years rather than outgrowing its spot. Evergreen, essentially pest-free, and never needs pruning beyond cutting spent bloom stalks. Plant it in drifts of three or five for the flower show, or single it where the spikes can be backlit.
red-yucca.bloom: Spring through fall (April – October), coral-red spikes, repeat blooming

flood-light.name: Flood Light
flood-light.description: A ground-mounted LED flood for washing walls, facades, and large trees with broad warm light. The head throws its wide beam well off vertical — place it a few feet back from the surface and use the rotation gesture to aim the wash. Switch to Night Mode to see it light up; in daylight it reads as a small dark fixture.

beaked-yucca.name: Beaked Yucca
beaked-yucca.origin: Chihuahuan Desert — West Texas and northern Mexico
beaked-yucca.description: The most architectural plant in the desert palette, and the one clients point at. A single smooth trunk carries a near-perfect sphere of stiff blue-green blades, each one finely toothed and tipped in gold, so the whole head catches low sun like a starburst. Unlike most yuccas it is genuinely tree-forming — old plants branch into candelabras — and unlike most it is cold-hardy well below anything Arizona sees, which is why it holds up in high-desert and mountain-town designs where agaves fail. Slow is the trade: a few inches of trunk a year, so buy the height you want rather than waiting for it. The blades are stiff but not dangerous, which makes it safe near walks and pool decks where an agave would not be. Give it hard drainage and full sun, plant it where it will be lit or backlit, and use it singly — this is a focal point, not a mass planting.
beaked-yucca.bloom: Late spring (May – June), creamy white panicle above the crown

aloe-vera.name: Aloe Vera
aloe-vera.description: One of the most recognizable succulents in the world, Aloe Vera forms a dense rosette of thick, fleshy leaves edged with small teeth. Extremely drought tolerant and low maintenance, it thrives in hot, dry climates and poor soils. The clear gel inside its leaves is widely used for skin care and minor burns. An excellent choice for desert landscapes, container gardens, and low-water designs.

purple-lantana.name: Purple Lantana
purple-lantana.description: The workhorse trailing lantana, and the one that carries colour through an Arizona summer when little else will. Low, fast, and relentlessly flowering — clusters of lavender-purple bloom from spring until frost with no deadheading — it spills over walls, boulders, and planter edges and knits into a dense weed-suppressing mat in a single season. It takes reflected heat off pavement and block walls without complaint, asks for poor soil and little water, and butterflies work it all day. Shear it back hard in late winter to clear frost damage and keep it from going woody in the middle; it rebounds fast. Evergreen in mild winters and root-hardy well below that.

ocotillo.name: Ocotillo
ocotillo.origin: Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts — Arizona, southern California, Texas and northern Mexico
ocotillo.description: A fountain of whip-like canes rising from a single crown, and the most sculptural line in the desert palette. Ocotillo is leafless and gray most of the year — that is the plant, not a problem — then leafs out within days of rain in a coat of small bright-green leaves and drops them again when the soil dries, repeating several times a season. In spring every cane tips in a flame of tubular red-orange flowers that hummingbirds fight over. Use it as a vertical exclamation against a wall or the sky, in a group of three at different heights, or planted close as a living fence (the canes root and the spines do the rest). It is sold bare root by height, and the one thing it asks is patience: a transplant can take a full season or two to leaf reliably. Full sun, sharp drainage, essentially no water once established, and cold-hardy to about 10 °F.
ocotillo.bloom: Spring (March – June), red-orange cane tips; flushes of leaves after any rain

aloe-ferox.name: Aloe Ferox
aloe-ferox.origin: South Africa — Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal
aloe-ferox.description: The big architectural aloe, and the one that reads as a specimen from across a yard. Thick blue-green leaves armed with reddish teeth spiral into a rosette that can span six feet, and with age the plant lifts itself onto a single bare trunk skirted in dried leaves. In midwinter — when almost nothing else in a desert garden is working — it throws candelabra spikes of hot orange-red flowers three feet above the foliage, and hummingbirds find them immediately. It is the source of the bitter aloe used medicinally, tougher and far more cold-hardy than Aloe vera, and it wants full sun, fast drainage, and almost no summer water once established. Give it room and a clear sightline; this is a plant to place deliberately, not to repeat.

gray-boulder.name: Gray Boulder
gray-boulder.description: A weathered gray granite boulder that adds natural texture and grounding weight to desert landscapes. Used as a focal point, border accent, or dry riverbed element. Boulders pair well with ornamental grasses, agave, and low-water perennials to create authentic Sonoran compositions. Zero maintenance once placed.

moroccan-mound.name: Moroccan Mound
moroccan-mound.description: A dense, clumping succulent that forms a low mound of upright, four-angled blue-green columns edged with small teeth. Native to the rocky slopes of Morocco's Atlas Mountains, Euphorbia resinifera is exceptionally heat and drought tolerant and spreads slowly into a broad cushion over time. Its architectural, coral-like massing makes a bold textural focal point among boulders, gravel, and other low-water desert plantings. Contains a caustic latex sap — site it away from high-traffic areas and handle with care.

tropical-agave.name: Tropical Agave
tropical-agave.description: A bold, open-rosette agave with long, narrow, recurving blades that arch outward for a lush, tropical-looking silhouette. Its loose, spreading form softens the hard architecture of desert plantings and pairs beautifully with boulders, columnar cacti, and fine gravel. Each blade tapers to a fine point and catches light along its length. Exceptionally drought and heat tolerant, it thrives in full sun and well-drained soil with virtually no maintenance once established.

firestick.name: Firestick
firestick.description: A striking, sculptural succulent made up of dense, pencil-thin cylindrical stems that branch like coral. In full sun and cool weather the new growth flushes brilliant shades of orange, red, and gold — the trait behind its 'Sticks on Fire' name — cooling to yellow-green in shade and heat. Leafless and architectural, it makes a bold vertical accent in desert and modern landscapes and pairs beautifully with boulders and blue agaves. Extremely heat and drought tolerant. Caution: the milky sap is a strong skin and eye irritant, so site it away from high-traffic areas and handle with gloves.

white-dawn-lantana.name: White Dawn Lantana
white-dawn-lantana.description: A low, fast-spreading trailing lantana smothered in clean white flower clusters from spring until frost. It cascades beautifully over walls, boulders, and planter edges, and fills in quickly as a tough sun-loving groundcover that shrugs off reflected heat and poor soil. Butterflies work it constantly. Shear it back hard in late winter to keep it dense and to clear any frost damage — it rebounds fast. Reliably evergreen in mild winters and root-hardy well below that.
